name: Analog stick dead zone
summary: Ignore tiny stick readings near the center, then rescale the rest so movement still starts smoothly from zero.
what_it_does: Analog sticks rarely rest at exactly zero. Worn or loose sticks report a small value when nobody touches them, and the character creeps. A dead zone treats readings under a threshold as zero. Rescaling the rest of the range back to 0 to 1 avoids a jump in speed at the edge of the dead zone. This demo simulates a drifting stick with the keyboard: the arrow keys push a virtual stick that has some drift built in.
use_when: Any game that reads analog sticks or triggers.
watch_out: Too large a dead zone makes small, precise moves impossible. Test with a real controller.
starting_values: Josh Sutphin's article on dead zones puts the usual threshold between 0.1 and 0.2 and recommends a scaled radial dead zone for 2D stick input.
prompt:
Add a dead zone to analog stick input.
- Read the stick as a 2D vector. If its length is under 0.2, treat it as zero.
- Otherwise rescale: direction * (length - 0.2) / (1 - 0.2), so output starts at 0 at the dead zone edge and reaches 1 at full tilt.
- Apply it to the vector, not to each axis separately, so diagonals stay smooth.
- Make the threshold a setting.

Acceptance checks:
1. A resting stick with drift under the threshold moves nothing.
2. Pushing just past the dead zone gives a small speed, not a jump.
3. Full tilt still reaches full speed.

sources.title: Doing Thumbstick Dead Zones Right (Josh Sutphin, archived copy)
